title: AI was probably involved in recent tech outages — just not in the way you expect
excerpt: Major US banks, Microsoft, and the FAA all faced recent tech outages. A rush to fix cybersecurity flaws discovered by AI may be contributing.

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

A spate of high-profile tech outages has people wondering if AI is to blame. They might be on the right track.

Organizations have been using AI to discover software vulnerabilities in their systems, then rolling out a higher-than-normal volume of fixes that may have overwhelmed them, politicians and tech executives have said.

"We're updating to withstand and be more resilient, and sometimes you do that at a speed where you couldn't test all the potential outcomes of the update," Kevin Mandia, the CEO of cybersecurity company Armadin, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday.

In the last five days, tech outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have caused major disruption for businesses and consumers. A temporary ground stop at every airport in America also caused mass chaos, though Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed aging air traffic control infrastructure for the issue.

While tech outages have long occurred periodically, the proximity of recent incidents has led many to speculate whether they were a coordinated cyberattack, rogue AI, or a combination of the two.

AI can discover cyber vulnerabilities that have remained undetected for years in human-made, occasionally sloppy software. There are also concerns that the technology could be used to exploit security flaws more quickly than humans ever could. Both these fears appear to have prompted companies to patch things more than usual, which in some cases may have caused things to break.

Organizations will likely continue to update their software at a faster rate, Mandia said. That will, in turn, probably lead to more tech outages, he added.

"Nobody wants an outage," he said. "Everybody's going to get operationally better at updating in the AI age. We're just at the first inning of this."

The near-term cybersecurity pain, he said, will likely result in long-term gains.

More tech outages?

Sen. Mark Warner, the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, reiterated assurances from other government officials that the tech outages weren't the result of a coordinated cyberattack by another country or malicious actor.

Warner also told CNBC on Wednesday that AI tools can identify software vulnerabilities in existing tech stacks, prompting a "mad rush" to create patches quickly.

"When that happens, careless things happen, the system can't absorb those patches as quickly, and you have these series of outages that have taken place. I think we will see more," Warner said.

Nicole Perlroth, a former cybersecurity reporter and founder of a cybersecurity-focused venture capital fund, said in an X post that new pressure to patch issues and update software faster means those fixes are more likely to "break things in unexpected, cascading ways."

The widespread cybersecurity horrors picked up steam last month, after AI discovered huge flaws in a programming language that up to 70% of websites use. Since then, there have been a crypto heist, refrigerator hacks, and attempts to literally boil blood.
